references.text: The parallel passage in the Sermon on the Mount: "And which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life?" ([ref:Matt 6:27|Matthew 6:27]). Jesus asks the same rhetorical question to show that worry is useless.

The psalmist reflects on the brevity of life: "Behold, you have made my days a few handbreadths, and my lifetime is as nothing before you. Surely all mankind stands as a mere breath" ([ref:Sal 39:5-6|Psalms 39:5-6]). Humans cannot extend their fixed lifespan by their own power.

The immediate context in Matthew's parallel where Jesus exhorts the disciples not to worry about life, food, or clothing, and points to the birds that God provides for ([ref:Matt 6:25-26|Matthew 6:25-26]).

The close context in Luke where Jesus says that life is more than food and the body more than clothing, and refers to the ravens whom God feeds ([ref:Luk 12:22-24|Luke 12:22-24]). Worry is unnecessary because God cares for His own.

The following verse where Jesus concludes: "If you cannot do even the least thing, why are you anxious about the rest?" ([ref:Luk 12:26|Luke 12:26]). The point is reinforced – when humans cannot influence even the smallest things, worry is meaningless.

"Commit your way to the Lord; trust in him, and he will act" ([ref:Sal 37:5|Psalms 37:5]). Instead of worrying, humans should entrust everything to God, who has power over the length of life and circumstances.

"When his days are determined, when the number of his months is with you, when you have set a limit he cannot pass" ([ref:Job 14:5|Job 14:5]). Human lifespan is fixed by God and cannot be extended by human worry.

Paul encourages not to worry but to present everything to God in prayer: "Do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God" ([ref:Fil 4:6-7|Philippians 4:6-7]). The New Testament answer to worry is trust in God.
"Cast all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you" ([ref:1 Pet 5:7|1 Peter 5:7]). Peter's exhortation confirms Jesus' teaching that worry should be entrusted to God.
